title: The Ascetic Prince: Saeed ibn Amir al-Jumahi
subtitle: The story of the youth who witnessed the execution of Khubayb (may Allah be pleased with him) and was guided, living as an ascetic prince who feared worldly distractions for his Hereafter.
heroQuote: "Saeed ibn Amir is a man who traded the Hereafter for the world and preferred Allah and His Messenger over all else."
intention: Read today's journey to contemplate how faith can transform a witness into a leader, and how worldly asceticism is the key to ultimate salvation in the Hereafter.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: The young Saeed ibn Amir al-Jumahi (may Allah be pleased with him) was one of the thousands of Quraysh who went out to the area of al-Tan'eem to witness the execution of Khubayb ibn Adi (may Allah be pleased with him), a companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, after trapping him treacherously. His vibrant youth and flowing vigor allowed him to push his way through the crowd until he stood shoulder-to-shoulder with the elders and chieftains of Quraysh, to witness this harrowing event that would change the course of his life forever.

steps.type: From Witness to Amir of Homs
steps.title: From Witness to Amir of Homs
steps.content:
Saeed ibn Amir stood tall, looking out at Khubayb (may Allah be pleased with him) as he was led to the execution cross. He heard his steady, calm voice saying, 'If you wish to let me pray two rak'ahs before my execution, then do so...' He then saw him face the Kaaba, pray two rak'ahs, and say, 'By Allah, were it not that you would think I prolonged the prayer out of fear of death, I would have prayed much more.' He witnessed his people mutilating Khubayb alive, cutting piece after piece from his body, asking him, 'Would you like Muhammad to be in your place while you are safe?' Khubayb replied while bleeding, 'By Allah, I would not wish to be safe and sound with my family and children while Muhammad is pricked by a thorn.' Then Saeed watched Khubayb raise his gaze to the sky from above the cross and say, 'O Allah, count them in numbers, destroy them scattered, and do not leave a single one of them.'

Khubayb never left Saeed's mind; he saw him in his dreams and waking moments, hearing the echo of his voice invoking against Quraysh. Khubayb taught him that true life is creed and striving, that firm faith works wonders, and that a man loved so deeply by his companions must indeed be a Prophet supported from the heavens. At that moment, Allah opened Saeed ibn Amir's heart to Islam, and he stood before a gathering of people to declare his dissociation from the sins and burdens of Quraysh and his entry into the religion of Allah. He migrated to Medina, attached himself to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and witnessed Khaybar and subsequent battles.

When the Prophet ﷺ passed away to the mercy of his Lord, Saeed remained a drawn sword in the hands of his two Caliphs, Abu Bakr and Umar. Entering upon Umar ibn al-Khattab at the beginning of his caliphate, he said, 'O Umar, I advise you to fear Allah regarding the people, and do not fear the people regarding Allah, and let not your speech contradict your action, for the best of speech is that which is confirmed by action...' Umar then appointed him over Homs, and Saeed initially refused out of fear of temptation, but Umar insisted.

After a time, the people of Homs came to Umar complaining about their Amir, Saeed, with four grievances: he does not come out to them until late in the morning, he does not answer anyone at night, he does not come out to them one day a month, and he suffers from fainting spells causing him to tune out from his gathering. Saeed answered every complaint by revealing his asceticism and piety: he wakes up in the morning to knead dough for his family because they have no servant, he makes the day for the people and the night for Allah, he washes his only garment once a month and waits for it to dry, and the fainting spell hits him to remind him of the execution of Khubayb (may Allah be pleased with him) and how he failed to help him when he was a polytheist. Umar wept and said, 'Praise be to Allah Who did not let my opinion of him down.'

When Umar sent him a thousand dinars to help with his needs, Saeed refused and said to his wife, 'The world has entered upon me to ruin my Hereafter, and temptation has settled in my house.' When his wife asked him how to get rid of it, he distributed it among the poor Muslims, saying, 'We lend it to Allah as a goodly loan.'

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The profound impact of sincere spiritual moments: how a single event can change a person's life and guide them.
2. True worldly asceticism: Saeed ibn Amir (may Allah be pleased with him) set the finest example of detachment from wealth and status, preferring the Hereafter over this world.
3. Responsible and transparent leadership: despite his status as an Amir, Saeed (may Allah be pleased with him) served his family himself, endured hardships, and faced complaints with honesty and clarity.
4. The power of faith in facing trials: Saeed (may Allah be pleased with him) never forgot Khubayb's execution, turning it into a driving force to remain steadfast on the truth and hold himself accountable for his past shortcomings.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: How can a single moment completely change the course of your life? What is the event that deeply touched you and changed your perspective on life? Are you ready to sacrifice your comfort and worldly gains for the sake of Allah?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Give charity today with something you love, or provide a service to those in need, following the example of Saeed ibn Amir (may Allah be pleased with him) in his altruism and asceticism, remembering that every good deed is a goodly loan with Allah.

title: The Light of Da'wah: At-Tufayl ibn Amr ad-Dawsi
subtitle: The story of the chieftain of Daws who was guided by the light of the Quran, returning to his people as a caller carrying the light of a miracle.
heroQuote: "O Allah, grant him a sign that will aid him in what he intends of good."
intention: Read today's journey to contemplate how a sincere word can pierce hearts, and how eloquence and wisdom are keys to calling people to Allah.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: At-Tufayl ibn Amr ad-Dawsi (may Allah be pleased with him) was the chieftain of the Daws tribe during the pre-Islamic era (Jahiliyyah), a distinguished noble among the Arabs, and renowned for his chivalry. His cooking pots were never lifted from the fire, nor was his door ever closed to a traveler; he fed the hungry, secured the frightened, and granted sanctuary to the refugee. In addition, he was a refined, intelligent literateur and a sensitive poet, deeply appreciative of eloquent speech where words acted like magic.

steps.type: From Blocking Ears to the Light of Guidance
steps.title: From Blocking Ears to the Light of Guidance
steps.content:
At-Tufayl left the lands of his people in Tihamah heading toward Mecca, where the struggle was raging between the Noble Prophet ﷺ and the disbelievers of Quraysh. As soon as the chieftains of Quraysh saw him, they welcomed him and gathered around him, warning him against Muhammad ﷺ. They said, 'O Tufayl, you have come to our land, and this man who claims to be a prophet has disrupted our affairs, torn our unity, and scattered our community. We fear that what has befallen us might befall you and your leadership among your people. So do not speak to the man, and do not listen to anything from him, for he has speech like magic that separates a son from his father, a brother from his brother, and a husband from his wife.'

By Allah, they continued pressing him with strange tales and warning him for his own safety and that of his people, until he resolved not to approach him or listen to anything from him. When he went to the mosque to circumambulate the Kaaba, he stuffed his ears with cotton for fear that some of Muhammad's words might reach him. Yet as soon as he entered the mosque, he found him ﷺ standing praying near the Kaaba in a manner different from theirs, worshipping in a way unlike their worship. His appearance captivated him, his worship moved him, and he found himself drawing closer and closer to him until he was near him. Allah willed that some of what he was saying reach his ears, and he heard fine speech.

He said to himself, 'May your mother bereave you, O Tufayl! You are an intelligent poet, and the good and bad are not hidden from you. What prevents you from hearing what this man says? If what he brings is good, you accept it, and if it is bad, you leave it.' He waited until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to his home, then followed him inside and said, 'O Muhammad, your people said to me such and such... By Allah, they kept warning me about your matter until I stuffed my ears with cotton so I would not hear your speech, but Allah willed that I hear some of it, and I found it good. So present your affair to me.' The Prophet ﷺ presented Islam to him and recited Surah al-Ikhlas and al-Falaq. By Allah, he had never heard speech better than his, nor seen a matter more just than his. At that, he extended his hand, testified that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and entered Islam.

At-Tufayl stayed in Mecca for a time, learning the matters of Islam and memorizing what was easy for him of the Quran. When he intended to return to his people, he said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a man obeyed among my clan, and I am returning to them to call them to Islam. So pray to Allah to grant me a sign that will be a helper for me in what I call them to.' The Prophet ﷺ said, 'O Allah, grant him a sign.' At-Tufayl set out toward his people, and when he reached a high place overlooking their homes, a light shone between his eyes like a lamp. He said, 'O Allah, place it other than on my face, for I fear they will think it is a punishment that befell my face for abandoning their religion.' The light shifted and settled on the tip of his whip, so people watched that light on his whip like a hanging lantern as he descended toward them.

When he arrived, his father—who was an old man—came to him. At-Tufayl said to him, 'Keep away from me, O father; I am not from you and you are not from me.' He asked, 'Why, my son?' He replied, 'I have embraced Islam and followed the religion of Muhammad ﷺ.' His father said, 'My son, my religion is your religion.' So he embraced Islam. Then his wife came and embraced Islam as well. Then At-Tufayl called the Daws tribe, but they were slow to respond except for Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who was the quickest of people to embrace Islam.

At-Tufayl returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Mecca along with Abu Hurayrah. The Prophet ﷺ asked him, 'What is behind you, O Tufayl?' He replied, 'Hearts covered with thick veils and intense disbelief... Daws has been overcome by sin and disobedience.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up, performed ablution, prayed, and raised his hands to the sky. Abu Hurayrah feared that he would invoke against them and they would perish, but the Prophet ﷺ began saying, 'O Allah, guide Daws... O Allah, guide Daws... O Allah, guide Daws.' Then he turned to At-Tufayl and said, 'Return to your people, be gentle with them, and call them to Islam.'

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The power of the Noble Quran: how hearing a few verses of the Quran was enough to open the heart of At-Tufayl (may Allah be pleased with him) to Islam despite all warnings.
2. Wisdom in calling to Allah: At-Tufayl (may Allah be pleased with him) did not despair of his people; rather, he called them with gentleness and wisdom, following the instruction of the Prophet ﷺ.
3. Divine miracles: The sign that appeared to At-Tufayl (may Allah be pleased with him) was a helper in his da'wah and a confirmation of the truth of Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ prophethood.
4. The impact of leaders on their societies: At-Tufayl's (may Allah be pleased with him) acceptance of Islam had a profound effect on his family and people, demonstrating the importance of exemplary leadership.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: What barriers do you sometimes place between yourself and the truth? How can you open your heart to hear good words and be moved by them? And how can you be a good role model in your call to goodness?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Look for a verse from the Noble Quran or a noble prophetic tradition today, deeply contemplate its meanings, and then try to share these meanings with those around you with wisdom and gentleness, following the example of At-Tufayl (may Allah be pleased with him).

title: The Rock of Faith in the Face of Tyrants
subtitle: The journey of Abdullah ibn Hudhafah as-Sahmi, from the Prophet's embassy to legendary resilience before the kings of the earth—a story of unyielding steadfastness.
emotion: Steadfastness, Courage, Honor in Islam, Sacrifice
heroQuote: "By Allah, if you were to give me all that you possess, and all that the Arabs possess, in order for me to turn back from the religion of Muhammad even for the blink of an eye, I would not do it" (may Allah be pleased with him).
intention: Read today's journey to contemplate the greatness of steadfastness upon the truth, the power of faith that defeats the arrogance of kings, and how a Muslim is honored through his religion.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Abdullah ibn Hudhafah as-Sahmi, a noble Companion, was not among those of prominent lineage and status in Jahiliyyah, but Islam elevated him and raised his status. He was among the foremost in Islam, known for his truthfulness, courage, and dedication to his religion. The Prophet ﷺ chose him for a momentous mission: carrying the message of Islam to the kings of the earth in a mission fraught with danger, yet it displayed the greatness of his faith and steadfastness.

steps.type: The Prophet's Ambassador and His Resilience Before Kings
steps.title: The Prophet's Ambassador and His Resilience Before Kings
steps.content:
In the sixth year of Hijrah, the Prophet ﷺ resolved to send his messengers to the non-Arab kings, calling them to Islam. It was a perilous mission; the messengers would travel to distant lands, ignorant of their languages and the temperaments of their kings, inviting them to abandon their religions and authority. The Prophet ﷺ chose six Companions for this task, and Abdullah ibn Hudhafah as-Sahmi was one of them, chosen to carry the letter of the Prophet ﷺ to Khosrow, the King of Persia.

Abdullah prepared his mount, bid farewell to his family and children, and set off alone with no one except Allah, until he reached the lands of Persia. He asked permission to enter upon Khosrow, who ordered his royal hall to be decorated and summoned the nobles of Persia. Abdullah ibn Hudhafah entered upon Khosrow in simple garments, yet his head was held high, his posture upright, radiating the honor of Islam burning in his heart.

When Khosrow saw him, he gestured to one of his men to take the letter, but Abdullah refused, saying, "No, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded me to hand it directly to you, and I will not disobey an order from the Messenger of Allah." Khosrow permitted him to approach and he handed him the letter. Khosrow summoned an Arab scribe to read it, and it stated: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Khosrow, the Great of Persia. Peace be upon the one who follows guidance..."

As soon as Khosrow heard this much, fires of rage ignited in his chest, his face reddened, and his veins swelled because the Prophet ﷺ had mentioned himself first. He grabbed the letter and tore it to pieces, shouting, "Does he write this to me, while he is my slave?!" Then he ordered Abdullah to be driven out of his assembly. Abdullah left, not knowing what Allah would do with him—would he be killed or left free? But he quickly said, "By Allah, I do not care what condition I am in after I have delivered the letter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

When Abdullah came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him of what Khosrow did and how he tore the letter, the Prophet ﷺ said, "May Allah tear apart his kingdom." And indeed, it was not long before a letter arrived from Sheroyah (Khosrow's son) to Badan (Khosrow's deputy in Yemen) informing him of Khosrow's assassination. Upon that, Badan announced his entry into Islam, along with the Persians who were with him in Yemen.

During the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Abdullah ibn Hudhafah was taken prisoner by the Romans. Caesar, the King of Rome, ordered his men to bring him alive. Caesar looked at Abdullah for a long time, then offered him Christianity, promising to set him free and honor his status. Abdullah replied with pride and firmness, "Far be it... death is a thousand times dearer to me than what you are calling me to."

Caesar offered to share his authority and wealth with him if he became a Christian, to which the captive smiled and said, "By Allah, if you were to give me all that you possess, and all that the Arabs possess, in order for me to turn back from the religion of Muhammad even for the blink of an eye, I would not do it." Upon that, Caesar ordered him to be crucified, commanding his archers to shoot near his hands and feet while offering him Christianity, but he refused.

Then Caesar ordered him to be taken down and called for a massive cauldron filled with oil, heated over fire until it boiled. He brought two Muslim prisoners, ordering one of them to be thrown into it, whereupon his flesh melted down to his bones. Then he turned to Abdullah and invited him to Christianity, but he remained even more firm in his refusal. Despairing of him, Caesar ordered him to be thrown into the cauldron. As he was being led away, his eyes teared up. Caesar thought he had panicked and ordered him brought back. When he stood before him, Caesar offered him Christianity again, and he refused.

Caesar asked, "Woe to you, what made you weep then?!" He replied, "I wept because I said to myself: You are about to be thrown into this cauldron right now, and your soul will depart, while I had wished that I had as many souls as the hairs on my body, and that I could throw them all into this cauldron in the way of Allah." The tyrant then said, "Would you accept to kiss my head and I will set you free?" Abdullah said, "And all the Muslim prisoners as well?" He said, "And all the Muslim prisoners as well."

Abdullah approached and kissed his head, and the Roman king ordered all the Muslim prisoners to be gathered and handed over to him. Abdullah ibn Hudhafah arrived back to Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) and told him his story. The Farooq (Umar) was immensely pleased, and when he looked at the prisoners, he said, "It is incumbent upon every Muslim to kiss the head of Abdullah ibn Hudhafah, and I will start with that." He then stood up and kissed his head (may Allah be pleased with him).

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. A Muslim's honor in his religion: Abdullah ibn Hudhafah (may Allah be pleased with him) showed unmatched dignity before the greatest king of the earth, holding firmly to his faith.
2. Steadfastness upon principles: Despite threats of death and torture, he did not compromise his faith an iota, standing like an unyielding rock against tyranny.
3. Zeal for Muslims: He was not content with saving only himself; rather, he conditioned his release on freeing all Muslim prisoners, showing his noble character.
4. The nobility of martyrdom: His wish to have souls equal to the number of his hairs to die as a martyr in the path of Allah reflects the depth of his faith and longing for the Hereafter.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: In which situations do I find myself compromising my principles out of fear or greed? And how can I draw inspiration from Abdullah ibn Hudhafah's steadfastness (may Allah be pleased with him) to be more courageous in upholding the truth?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Today, I will strive to speak the truth and defend it, even if it contradicts a personal interest, and I will pray to Allah for steadfastness upon His religion.

title: From the Darkness of Hatred to the Light of Faith
subtitle: The journey of Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi, from a plot to assassinate the Prophet ﷺ to a sincere embrace of Islam, a profound transformation of the heart.
heroQuote: "Umayr ibn Wahb became dearer to me than some of my own sons." - Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him)
intention: Read today's journey to reflect on the vastness of Allah's mercy, His ability to guide hearts, and how a human being can transform from a fierce enemy into a sincere friend.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi was one of the prominent chieftains and brave warriors of Quraysh, and one of the fiercest enemies of Islam in its early days. He participated in the Battle of Badr against the Muslims, returning from it to leave behind his son Wahb as a captive in the hands of the Muslims. He harbored deep-seated hatred in his heart against the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims, and worries overwhelmed him due to his debts and the captivity of his son, which drove him to contemplate a monumental deed.

steps.type: A Failed Plot and Divine Guidance
steps.title: A Failed Plot and Divine Guidance
steps.content:
Umayr ibn Wahb al-Jumahi returned from Badr having saved his own life, but he left behind his son Wahb captive in the hands of the Muslims. He feared that the Muslims would punish the young man for his father's actions and subject him to severe torment as retribution for the harm he had once inflicted upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One morning, Umayr headed to the Sacred Mosque to tawaf around the Kaaba and seek blessings from its idols, and found Safwan ibn Umayya sitting near the Hijr.

Umayr greeted Safwan with a pre-Islamic greeting, and then they sat reminiscing about Badr and its great tragedy, listing the captives who had fallen into the hands of Muhammad and his companions. Safwan sighed and said, 'By Allah, there is no goodness in life after them.' Umayr replied, 'You have spoken the truth, by Allah.' Then he remained silent for a moment and said in a low voice, 'By the Lord of the Kaaba, were it not for debts upon me that I have no means to pay, and a family I fear would be lost after me, I would set out to Muhammad and kill him, settle his affair, and rid you of his evil. Indeed, the presence of my son Wahb among them makes my going to Yathrib a matter that would not arouse suspicion.'

Safwan ibn Umayya seized upon Umayr's words and was unwilling to let this opportunity slip away. He turned to him and said, 'O Umayr, make all your debts my responsibility; I will pay them off for you no matter how much they amount to... As for your family, I will integrate them into my own family for as long as I and they live, and my wealth is vast enough to accommodate them all and ensure them a luxurious life.' Umayr said, 'Then conceal this conversation of ours and do not let anyone know.' Safwan replied, 'You have my word.'

Umayr arose from the mosque with the fires of hatred blazing in his heart against Muhammad ﷺ, and he began preparing to execute what he had resolved, heading towards Madinah. When he arrived in Madinah, Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him) saw him, recognized him, seized him, and brought him before the Prophet ﷺ. When the Prophet ﷺ asked him the reason for his coming, Umayr tried to pretend that he had come to seek the ransom for his son, but the Prophet ﷺ exposed his plot with Safwan ibn Umayya, recounting to him the details of their private conversation which no one else had heard except Allah.

At that moment, Umayr's heart trembled, and he bore witness that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, declaring his Islam. This moment marked the turning point in his life, as he transformed from a bitter enemy into a sincere believer. He asked the Prophet ﷺ to permit him to return to Makkah to invite Safwan and Quraysh to Islam, and he granted him permission. Umayr returned to Makkah calling people to Allah, and many embraced Islam at his hands. Umayr ibn Wahb became one of the finest Companions, to the extent that Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him) said of him: 'Umayr ibn Wahb became dearer to me than some of my own sons.'

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The vastness of Allah's mercy and His mighty power to guide hearts: How Allah guides whom He wills, even the fiercest of enemies.
2. The miracle of the Prophet ﷺ and his knowledge of the unseen: The Prophet's informing Umayr of the details of his plot was conclusive proof of his prophethood.
3. The importance of sincere repentance: Umayr's transformation from intending murder to becoming a caller to Islam highlights the power of repentance.
4. The positive transformation in a Muslim's life: How Islam can radically change a person for the better, making them one of the best of people.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: Do I truly believe that Allah is capable of changing any heart, no matter how harsh or distant it may seem? And how can I be a cause for the guidance of others, or accept Allah's guidance for myself at any moment?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Today, I will pray to Allah for guidance for myself and those I love, and I will take care never to despair of anyone's guidance, remembering the story of Umayr ibn Wahb (May Allah be pleased with him).

title: Al-Baraa ibn Malik: The Champion of Martyrdom and the Key to the Garden of Death
subtitle: The story of the slender Companion who terrified enemies with his supreme courage and dedication in the path of Allah.
heroQuote: "O assembly of the Ansar, let none of you think of returning to Madinah; there is no Madinah for you after today... There is only Allah alone... then Paradise."
intention: Read today's journey to draw inspiration from the courage and fearlessness of Al-Baraa ibn Malik, to reflect on the value of self-sacrifice in the path of Allah, and the sincerity of seeking martyrdom.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Al-Baraa ibn Malik al-Ansari, the brother of the servant of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Anas ibn Malik, was a slender-bodied man with disheveled hair, whom the eye would scarcely notice. Yet behind this frail appearance lay the heart of a lion that knew no fear, and a bold spirit that did not dread death. Such was the extent of his bravery and daring that the Farooq, Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him), wrote to his governors across the regions: 'Do not appoint Al-Baraa as a commander over any Muslim army, for fear that he might destroy his troops out of his sheer daring.' Despite this, Al-Baraa killed a hundred polytheists in single combat, aside from those he killed in the thick of battle.

steps.type: A Failed Plot and Divine Guidance
steps.title: The Garden of Death and Seeking Martyrdom
steps.content:
After the death of the Prophet ﷺ, many Arab tribes apostatized, the strongest of the apostates being Banu Hanifa, the followers of Musaylimah the Liar, who had amassed forty thousand fierce warriors. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (May Allah be pleased with him) sent an army led by Khalid ibn al-Walid (May Allah be pleased with him), and Al-Baraa ibn Malik was in the vanguard of this army.

The two armies met in Al-Yamamah, the battle intensified, and the Muslims' fortunes initially waned until Musaylimah's men breached the tent of Khalid ibn al-Walid. At that moment, the Muslims felt imminent danger, and Khalid rushed to reorganize the ranks. Khalid turned to Al-Baraa and said, 'To them, O young man of the Ansar.' Al-Baraa turned to his people, the Ansar, and uttered his immortal statement: 'O assembly of the Ansar, let none of you think of returning to Madinah; there is no Madinah for you after today... There is only Allah alone... then Paradise.'

Then Al-Baraa charged at the polytheists and they charged with him, cleaving through the ranks with his sword until the footing of Musaylimah and his companions was shaken, forcing them to retreat into the Garden of Death—a garden with high walls whose gates they locked while showering the Muslims with arrows. Al-Baraa ibn Malik stepped forward and said, 'O people, place me on a shield, raise the shield upon spears, and then toss me into the garden near its gate. Either I will achieve martyrdom, or I will open the gate for you.'

In the blink of an eye, Al-Baraa sat on a shield, dozens of spears lifted it up, and they cast him inside the Garden of Death among thousands of apostates. He descended upon them like a thunderbolt, fighting fiercely by the gate with his sword until he killed ten of them and opened the door, sustaining over eighty wounds from arrow shots and sword blows. The Muslims surged forward, wielding their swords against the necks of the apostates until they killed nearly twenty thousand of them and struck down Musaylimah. Al-Baraa was carried back to his tent to be treated, and Khalid stayed with him for a month until Allah granted him recovery.

Al-Baraa continued to yearn for martyrdom, plunging into battle after battle. On the day of the conquest of Tustar in the lands of Persia, the Persians fortified themselves in their castles and cast down iron chains with glowing hooks that attached to the bodies of the Muslims. Hooks caught onto his brother Anas ibn Malik, and as soon as Al-Baraa saw him, he leaped onto the fortress wall, grabbed the chain holding his brother, and worked on the hooks to pull them out of his flesh. His hand was burned and smoked until it became bare bone without flesh, but he saved his brother. In this battle, Al-Baraa prayed to Allah to bless him with martyrdom, and Allah answered his prayer, falling as a martyr, joyfully meeting his Lord.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. Absolute courage in the path of Allah: Al-Baraa ibn Malik represents the peak of boldness and self-sacrifice for the victory of the religion.
2. Altruism and love of martyrdom: His preference for death over life, his request to be cast inside the Garden of Death, and his sacrifice of his hand to save his brother.
3. Steadfastness in the face of trials: His endurance and the Muslims' endurance during the Ridda wars, which almost eradicated Islam.
4. Inspirational leadership: His words that infused a spirit of enthusiasm into the Muslim army, turning defeat into victory.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: Reflect on your courage: Are you prepared to sacrifice what is dearest to you in the path of Allah? How can you be bolder and more steadfast in facing life's challenges and championing the truth?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Look for an opportunity today to be brave in speaking or acting upon the truth, even if it is difficult. Remember that boldness in the path of Allah begins with a small step of steadfastness.

title: Umm Salamah: The Patience of the Emigrant and Her Steadfastness on the Religion of Allah
subtitle: The journey of the Mother of the Believers who set the finest examples of patience and sacrifice for the sake of faith.
person: Umm Salamah Hind bint Abi Umayyah al-Makhzumiyyah
heroQuote: "When Abu Salamah resolved to set out for Madinah, he prepared a camel for me, mounted me upon it, placed our infant son Salamah in my lap, and set off leading the camel without looking back at anything."
intention: Read today's journey to reflect on the greatness of Umm Salamah's patience and steadfastness upon the religion of Allah, and to draw from her the strength of faith that makes all hardships and sacrifices seem trivial.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Umm Salamah, whose name was Hind bint Abi Umayyah, was one of the prominent noblewomen of Quraysh, and her husband, Abu Salamah Abdullah ibn Abd al-Asad, was among the foremost precursors to Islam. Umm Salamah and her husband embraced Islam early on, making them among the first to taste the bitterness of harm and persecution from Quraysh, which spared no effort in torturing and terrifying the Muslims. Yet her faith was as firm as mountains, neither weakening nor faltering in the face of severe torment.

steps.type: The Tragedy of Migration and Separation from Loved Ones
steps.title: The Tragedy of Migration and Separation from Loved Ones
steps.content:
When the persecution against the Muslims intensified, the Prophet ﷺ permitted his companions to emigrate to Abyssinia. Umm Salamah and her husband were among the first emigrants, leaving behind their homes and status in Makkah, reckoning all of that with Allah. Despite the protection given to them by the Negus, the yearning for Makkah and the cradle of revelation tore at their hearts. When news reached them of the conversion of Hamza and Umar, they returned to Makkah, only to discover that the persecution had worsened.

When the Prophet ﷺ permitted the migration to Madinah, Abu Salamah and Umm Salamah resolved to be the first emigrants. Abu Salamah prepared a camel, seated Umm Salamah and their infant son Salamah in her lap, and set off leading the camel. However, men from Umm Salamah's tribe, Banu Makhzum, intercepted their path and said to Abu Salamah, 'If you have conquered us regarding yourself, what about this wife of ours?! She is our daughter, how can we let you take her away from us and travel with her across the lands?' Thus, they snatched her away from him.

As soon as the men of Abu Salamah's tribe, Banu Abd al-Asad, saw them taking Umm Salamah and her child, they grew fiercely angry and said, 'No, by Allah, we will not leave the child with your companion after you snatched her away from our companion... He is our son and we have more right to him.' Thus, the family was torn apart: Banu Makhzum took Umm Salamah, Banu Abd al-Asad took her child Salamah, and Abu Salamah went off to Madinah alone. Umm Salamah wept for an entire year, going out every morning to Al-Abtah and weeping until evening, until some of her relatives took pity on her and allowed her to leave. She then retrieved her child after great effort and set off alone to Madinah to reunite with her husband after this immense ordeal, setting the finest example of patience and steadfastness upon the religion of Allah.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. Beautiful patience in trials: Umm Salamah's story embodies the utmost degrees of patience and steadfastness in the face of separation and hardship in the path of Allah.
2. Sacrifice for creed: Her repeated migrations, sacrifice of her home, family, and separation from her husband and child, were all for the sake of preserving her religion.
3. The strength of individual faith: Her faith did not waver despite loneliness and apparent weakness, indicating the depth of her belief in Allah.
4. The importance of the family in Islam: Despite the ordeal, the story demonstrates the value of family bonds and the importance of reuniting them in the path of Allah.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: Reflect on your trials: What are the greatest difficulties you have faced in your life? How did you react? Have you drawn inspiration from the patience of the righteous? And how can you increase your steadfastness and patience in facing daily life challenges?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Practice patience today in a difficult situation, or pray for your parents and family to remain steadfast on the truth, remembering that every trial you go through is an opportunity to strengthen your faith and patience.

title: The Patience of Umm al-Mu'minin Umm Salamah: From Separation to Meeting the Best of Creation
subtitle: A magnificent spiritual journey crowned with beautiful patience and contentment with Allah's decree, resulting in profound goodness.
person: Hind bint Abi Umayyah al-Makhzumiyyah (Umm Salamah) may Allah be pleased with her
heroQuote: "O Allah, with You I reckon this calamity of mine; O Allah, compensate me with something better than it."
intention: Read today's journey to reflect on how beautiful patience can transform hardships into blessings, and how contentment opens the doors of relief and abundant good.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: She is Hind bint Abi Umayyah al-Makhzumiyyah, one of the Mothers of the Believers and wives of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) was among the earliest to embrace Islam, migrating with her husband Abu Salamah (may Allah be pleased with him) to Abyssinia and then to Madinah. She faced numerous trials and tribulations for the sake of her religion, becoming a shining example of patience, steadfastness, and deep faith.

steps.type: The Tragedy of Migration and the Beauty of Divine Compensation
steps.title: The Tragedy of Migration and the Beauty of Divine Compensation
steps.content:
At a pivotal moment in the history of the Hijrah, Umm Salamah found her family torn apart. Her husband, Abu Salamah, had migrated to Madinah fleeing with his faith, while the clan of Banu Abd al-Asad snatched her son Salamah from her arms, and her own clan, Banu Makhzum, prevented her from leaving. She was separated from her husband and her son all in a single hour.

For a full year, Umm Salamah would go out every morning to al-Abtah, sitting at the very spot of her tragedy, reliving those painful moments and weeping until nightfall. Moved by her plight, a cousin from her tribe spoke to her people until they released her. Yet, she faced another dilemma: how could she join her husband while leaving the dearest piece of her heart behind in Makkah?

Once they returned her son Salamah to her, she did not hesitate. She prepared her camel, placed her child in her lap, and set off toward Madinah entirely alone, with no one accompanying her except Allah and her young son. Along the way, she met Uthman ibn Talhah (may Allah be pleased with him)—who was still a polytheist at the time—and he asked about her destination. When he learned she wanted to join her husband, he swore by Allah he would not leave her until she reached Madinah. Uthman ibn Talhah accompanied her with the most noble and honorable companionship. Whenever they stopped for rest, he would make her camel kneel, step away until she dismounted, and then prepare her resting place. When it was time to move, he would ready her mount, step back until she boarded, and then take the camel's nose-string to lead her.

Umm Salamah arrived at Quba, where her husband Abu Salamah was, and the family was finally reunited after a long separation. She lived with her husband and son in Madinah. Abu Salamah participated in the Battle of Badr and returned victorious, and later fought valiantly in the Battle of Uhud, where he sustained a severe wound. He treated it until he thought it had healed, but it flared up again and confined him to bed.

During his illness, Abu Salamah remembered a statement he heard from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "No calamity befalls a person who then responds by saying: 'O Allah, with You I reckon this calamity of mine; O Allah, compensate me with something better than it,' except that Allah the Almighty will grant it to him."

Days later, the Prophet ﷺ visited him, and no sooner had he departed than Abu Salamah passed away. The Prophet ﷺ gently closed his noble eyes and supplicated for him: "O Allah, forgive Abu Salamah, raise his rank among those drawn close to You, look after those he left behind among the survivors, forgive us and him, O Lord of the Worlds, make spacious his grave for him, and illuminate it for him."

Umm Salamah remembered her husband's supplication and said, "O Allah, with You I reckon this calamity of mine," but she hesitated to say, "O Allah, compensate me with something better than it," wondering within herself: 'Who could possibly be better than Abu Salamah?' Nevertheless, she completed the supplication.

The Muslims deeply grieved for her loss. Abu Bakr and Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) both proposed to her, but she declined. Then, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed to her. Umm Salamah apologized, citing her intense jealousy, her advanced age, and that she had young dependents. The Prophet ﷺ replied: "As for what you mentioned regarding your jealousy, I will pray to Allah the Almighty to remove it from you. As for your age, I have been afflicted with the same as you. And as for your dependents, your dependents are my dependents."

Thus, the Prophet ﷺ married her, and Allah answered her prayer, replacing Abu Salamah with someone far better. She became the Mother of the Believers, a mother to all the faithful. May Allah brighten her face in Paradise and be pleased with her.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. Beautiful patience and steadfastness upon the truth open the doors of relief and abundant goodness, even in the severest hardships.
2. Absolute trust in Allah the Almighty and contentment with His decree, knowing that He only brings what is good, even if it appears difficult in its outward form.
3. The immense virtue of supplication and turning to Allah during a calamity, for Allah rewards the patient with better than what they lost.
4. The noble character and mercy of the Prophet ﷺ, and how he served as the ultimate exemplar in caring for widows, dependents, and honoring the Companions.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: How do I receive the painful decrees of Allah in my life? Do I recall Umm Salamah's supplication during every hardship, fully convinced that Allah will compensate me with something better?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Sincerely invoke Allah during any difficulty using Umm Salamah's supplication: "O Allah, with You I reckon this calamity of mine; O Allah, compensate me with something better than it," and remember that after hardship comes ease.

title: From Enmity to Loyalty: The Islam of Thumamah ibn Uthal and the Blockade of Quraysh
subtitle: The story of a magnificent transformation of the chieftain of Yamamah, whose heart was illuminated by the light of Islam after intense hostility, becoming a drawn sword against the enemies of Allah.
person: Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi may Allah be pleased with him
heroQuote: "By Allah, there was no face on the surface of the earth more hateful to me than your face... but now your face has become the dearest of all faces to me."
intention: Read today's journey to reflect on how benevolent treatment can open closed hearts, and how Islam transforms souls from the depths of straying to the pinnacle of guidance.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi was a prominent chieftain of Banu Hanifah and one of the kings of Yamamah whose commands were unquestioned during the days of ignorance. When he received the letter of the Prophet ﷺ inviting him to Islam, he grew arrogant, turned away, harbored malice against the Prophet ﷺ, and attempted to assassinate him, prompting the Prophet to declare his blood forfeit among his companions.

steps.type: The Captive Whose Heart Was Illuminated by Faith
steps.title: The Captive Whose Heart Was Illuminated by Faith
steps.content:
Not long after, Thumamah resolved to perform Umrah, setting out from Yamamah toward Makkah. Along the way, he was intercepted by a patrol of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ patrolling the territory. They captured him—not knowing who he was—brought him to Madinah, and bound him to one of the pillars of the Mosque, awaiting the Prophet's verdict regarding him.

When the Prophet ﷺ came out to the mosque and saw Thumamah bound, he asked his companions, "Do you know whom you have captured?" They replied, "No, O Messenger of Allah." He said, "This is Thumamah ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, so treat his captivity well." The Prophet ﷺ then instructed his household to gather whatever food they had and send it to Thumamah, and ordered that his she-camel be milked for him morning and evening, with the milk delivered to him—all before the Prophet had even met or spoken to him.

Two days later, the Prophet ﷺ approached Thumamah, wishing to gently guide him to Islam, and asked him, "What do you have to say, O Thumamah?" Thumamah replied, "I have good to say, O Muhammad... If you kill me, you kill a person of blood (who deserves retaliation); if you show favor, you show favor to one who is grateful; and if you want wealth, ask and you shall be given whatever you wish." The Prophet ﷺ left him for two more days, during which food, drink, and camel's milk continued to be brought to him.

The following day, the Prophet ﷺ came to him and asked the same question: "What do you have to say, O Thumamah?" He gave the exact same reply. Thereupon, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ turned to his companions and said, "Release Thumamah." They untied his bonds and set him free.

Thumamah left the mosque and rode until he reached a grove of palm trees near the outskirts of Madinah. He made his camel kneel, bathed in the water there, purifying himself thoroughly, and then turned back toward the mosque. Upon reaching it, he stood before a gathering of Muslims and declared, "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger." He then walked up to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "O Muhammad, by Allah, there was no face on the surface of the earth more hateful to me than your face... but now your face has become the dearest of all faces to me. By Allah, there was no religion more hateful to me than your religion; but now your religion has become the dearest of all religions to me. By Allah, there was no land more hateful to me than your land; but now your land has become the dearest of all lands to me."

He then added, "I had shed blood among your companions; what is my liability for that?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, "There is no blame upon you today, O Thumamah; Islam erases what came before it," and gave him the glad tidings of the good that Allah had written for him through his Islam. Thumamah's face beamed with joy and he said, "By Allah, I shall inflict upon the polytheists manifold the harm I inflicted upon your companions, and I place myself, my sword, and my people at the service of you and your religion."

He then asked the Prophet ﷺ about performing the Umrah he had intended. The Prophet instructed him to proceed with his Umrah according to the way of Allah and His Messenger, and taught him the rites. Thumamah proceeded to Makkah, and when he reached its valley, he raised his voice in a resounding chant: "Labbayka Allahumma labbayk, labbayka la sharika laka labbayk..." He was the first Muslim to enter Makkah reciting the Talbiyah aloud.

Quraysh were seized with panic. As Thumamah approached them proclaiming the Talbiyah, they confronted him, but he declared, "I have not apostatized; rather, I have followed the best religion... By the Lord of this House, not a single grain of wheat or any provisions from Yamamah shall reach you after my return until you all follow Muhammad."

Thumamah completed his Umrah in full view of Quraysh, slaughtering his sacrifice for Allah rather than idols. He then returned to his land and ordered his people to cut off all trade and supplies to Quraysh. The blockade became so severe that Quraysh had to write to the Prophet ﷺ pleading with him to order Thumamah to release their provisions, whereupon the Prophet wrote to him, and he lifted the embargo.

Thumamah remained loyal to his religion and his covenant with his Prophet for the rest of his life. When the Prophet ﷺ passed away to the Highest Companion and the Arabs apostatized, Thumamah stood firm against Musaylimah the Liar among Banu Hanifah, fighting the apostates in jihad for the sake of Allah. May Allah reward him abundantly on behalf of Islam and the Muslims.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The sublime character of the Prophet ﷺ in dealing with captives and enemies, and how kindness serves as a key to softening stubborn hearts.
2. The power of Islam in transforming souls from extreme hostility to the highest loyalty and affection.
3. The importance of wisdom in calling others to Allah, exercising patience with invitees, and leaving hearts for Allah to turn however He wills.
4. Loyalty to covenants and steadfastness upon the truth, even in the face of trials and apostasy, as demonstrated by Thumamah in fighting the apostates.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: How can I apply the principle of benevolent treatment and mercy toward someone who disagrees with me in opinion or faith? Can I become a cause for guiding others through my good character and patience?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Look for an opportunity to show good character and mercy toward someone with whom you disagree. Remember that hearts are opened through gentleness rather than harshness, and that calling by example is more eloquent than words.

title: The Honor of Hospitality: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari and Hosting the Best of Creation
subtitle: A noble Companion who earned the supreme honor of hosting the Prophet ﷺ in his home, securing the pride of this world and the Hereafter, and a lofty status in the hearts of Muslims.
person: Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Kulayb (Abu Ayyub al-Ansari) may Allah be pleased with him
heroQuote: "Allah elevated his mention and exalted his status when He chose his house out of all the homes of the Muslims for the noble Prophet ﷺ to descend into."
intention: Read today's journey to reflect on the immense honor of serving the Prophet ﷺ, and how selflessness and sincere love elevate a person's standing in this world and the Hereafter.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: He is Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Kulayb, from the Banu an-Najjar, known by his kunyah Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him). He was a noble Companion among the finest of the Ansar. Allah elevated his mention and exalted his status across east and west when He chose his house above all the homes of the Muslims for the noble Prophet ﷺ to stay in when he arrived in Madinah as a migrant—an honor matched by no other.

steps.type: The Host of the Prophet ﷺ
steps.title: The Host of the Prophet ﷺ
steps.content:
When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah as an immigrant, the hearts of its people welcomed him with the warmest greeting a traveler could receive, and their eyes looked upon him with longing and affection. Every single Ansari desired the profound honor of hosting the Prophet ﷺ in his home, eagerly competing to take the reins of his noble camel and invite him inside.

However, the Prophet ﷺ, with his profound wisdom, let the camel walk wherever Allah commanded, saying, "Leave it, for it is commanded." The camel walked on until it knelt at the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (may Allah be pleased with him). This moment crowned Abu Ayyub with the immense honor of having the Prophet ﷺ as a guest in his home.

Joy flooded the hearts of Abu Ayyub and his wife, and they welcomed the Prophet ﷺ with utmost generosity. Abu Ayyub was deeply solicitous of the Prophet's comfort, assigning him the upper floor of the house. Yet, the Prophet ﷺ preferred the ground floor for the convenience of visitors. Abu Ayyub and his wife took great care never to walk above the Prophet's head, fulfilling every need to ensure his comfort and peace of mind.

Abu Ayyub al-Ansari lived a life filled with jihad and sacrifice for the sake of Allah, participating alongside the Prophet ﷺ in every single military campaign. He never missed a battle alongside the Muslims, continuing his service well into old age. He remained passionately devoted to jihad until he passed away as a warrior under the walls of Constantinople during the era of Mu'awiyah ibn Abi Sufyan (may Allah be pleased with him), and was buried there, fulfilling a wish he had expressed that his grave be at the farthest frontier of the lands of disbelief, serving as a permanent testament to the jihad of Muslims.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The immense honor of hosting the Prophet ﷺ, and how Allah chooses whom He wills among His servants to exalt their status and immortalize their memory.
2. Selflessness and sincere love for the Prophet ﷺ, as manifested in the eagerness of the Ansar to serve him and ensure his comfort.
3. The importance of striving in the way of striving (Jihad) steadfastly until the end of life, and seeking martyrdom for Allah's sake.
4. Generous hospitality and noble treatment, being hallmarks of true believers.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: How can I demonstrate my love for the Prophet ﷺ in my daily life? Do I serve my religion and the Muslims with selflessness and dedication, drawing inspiration from the generosity and sacrifice of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Give charity today with the intention of honoring a guest or assist someone in need, recalling the generosity and selflessness of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, and remember that honoring the guest is part of faith.

title: The Honor of Hosting the Prophet ﷺ: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari
subtitle: The journey of a noble Companion who attained the supreme honor of hosting the Best of Mankind in his home, weaving the finest tapestry of love and sacrifice.
heroQuote: "By Allah, neither I nor Ummu Ayyub closed our eyes in sleep that entire night. Could it be that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is on the lower floor while we are above him?!"
intention: Read today's journey to ponder the profound honor of hosting the Prophet ﷺ, and how love and sacrifice manifested in the life of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari (May Allah be pleased with him).

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, Khalid bin Zaid bin Kulayb (May Allah be pleased with him), was one of the noble leaders of the Ansar who believed in the Prophet ﷺ and supported him. He was distinguished by his generosity, munificence, and intense love for Islam and its Messenger. When the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Medina, the Ansar were eagerly awaiting the chance to host him, each hoping to attain this immense honor, but destiny had chosen a station for Abu Ayyub that no one else would attain.

steps.type: The Honor of the Prophet's Arrival in Abu Ayyub's Home
steps.title: The Honor of the Prophet's Arrival in Abu Ayyub's Home
steps.content:
When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Medina, after spending a few days in Quba, he set out riding his she-camel while all the leaders of Yathrib blocked his path, competing for the honor of hosting him. The Prophet ﷺ told them: "Leave her, for she is commanded." The camel continued to walk, with eyes following her and hearts surrounding her, until she knelt in front of the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari. The Prophet ﷺ did not dismount at first, then the camel leaped up and returned to kneel in the very same spot. Joy flooded Abu Ayyub's heart, and he rushed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, gathering his belongings and carrying them into his house.

Abu Ayyub's home consisted of two floors, upper and lower. Abu Ayyub cleared the upper floor for the Prophet ﷺ to stay in, but the Prophet ﷺ preferred the lower floor, and Abu Ayyub complied with his command. When night fell, Abu Ayyub and his wife went up to the upper floor, and no sooner had they closed the door than Abu Ayyub turned to his wife and said: "Woe to us, what have we done?! Can it be that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is below and we are above him?! Shall we walk above the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?! Shall we come between the Prophet and the Divine Revelation?! We would surely be ruined." They could not find peace until they moved to the side of the upper floor that did not lie directly over the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

On one cold night, a water jar broke on the upper floor, and Abu Ayyub and his wife hurried to dry the water using a velvet quilt they used as a blanket, out of fear that it might reach the Prophet ﷺ. When morning came, he told the Prophet ﷺ what had happened. The Prophet ﷺ accommodated him, moving up to the upper floor while Abu Ayyub moved to the lower floor. The Prophet ﷺ stayed in Abu Ayyub's house for about seven months, until his mosque and living quarters were built.

Abu Ayyub did not content himself with this honor alone; rather, he remained a warrior in the path of Allah throughout his life, and it is said he did not miss a single military campaign alongside the Muslims. His final expedition was the conquest of Constantinople when he was eighty years old, during which he fell ill, unable to fight. When Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah visited him during his illness, he asked, "Do you have any need, O Abu Ayyub?" He replied, "Convey my greetings to the Muslim armies, and tell them: Abu Ayyub advises you to advance as deep into the enemy's territory as possible, to carry him with you, and to bury him beneath your feet at the walls of Constantinople." He breathed his pure last breath, and the Muslim soldiers fulfilled his wish, burying him there as a witness to his profound love for Jihad.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The immense honor of hosting the Prophet ﷺ, and how Allah chooses whomever He wills for His great favor.
2. Sacrifice, asceticism in worldly matters, and love for the Prophet ﷺ that drives a person to offer what is most precious and valuable.
3. Consistency in striving and giving for the sake of Allah until one's final breath, without letting old age or illness hinder one.
4. Fulfilling covenants and good treatment, as manifested in his freeing of the female servant about whom the Prophet ﷺ had given good advice.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: How can we translate our love for the Prophet ﷺ into our daily lives, and make our homes and works places of his blessings and Sunnah?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Allocate a portion of your time today to read the biography of the Prophet ﷺ, reflect upon some of his Sunnahs to apply them in your life, or perform a purely charitable deed for the sake of Allah the Almighty.

title: Your Lame Leg in Paradise: Amr ibn al-Jamuh and His Longing for Martyrdom
subtitle: The story of an elderly lame man over sixty who insisted on treading Paradise with his limp, making his martyrdom the finest proof of his sincere faith.
emotion: Courage, Faith, Longing for Martyrdom, Sacrifice
heroQuote: "By Allah, I truly hope to tread into Paradise with this lame foot of mine!"
intention: Read today's journey to ponder the strength of faith that drives a person to overcome all obstacles, and how sincere intention elevates its holder to the highest ranks.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Amr ibn al-Jamuh (May Allah be pleased with him) was a leader among Banu Salamah in Yathrib and a prominent chief during the Jahiliyyah, renowned for his generosity and chivalry. He had a special idol named 'Manat' which he cared for deeply, seeking blessings through it and sacrificing for it. He was over sixty years old when the lights of faith began to illuminate the homes of Medina at the hands of Mus'ab ibn Umayr (May Allah be pleased with him).

steps.type: From Idol Worship to the Longing for Paradise
steps.title: From Idol Worship to the Longing for Paradise
steps.content:
Amr ibn al-Jamuh's three sons and his wife Hind embraced Islam in secret, knowing how deeply attached their father was to his idol. Recognizing that 'Manat's' standing in his heart was beginning to waver, they decided to remove it. Every night, his sons and Mu'adh ibn Jabal would go to the idol, carry it away, and throw it into a pit of filth. In the morning, Amr would find it turned upside down in the pit, wash it, perfume it, and return it to its place, threatening whoever had done it. This repeated for two nights, and on the third night, they hung a sword around the idol's neck and said, "O Manat, by Allah, I know not who is doing this to you that you see; if there is any good in you, defend yourself, and this sword is with you." When he fell asleep, the youths took the sword from the idol's neck, tied it to a dead dog, and threw them both into a well of filth. When Amr woke up and found his idol in that state, he realized the truth and began reciting: "By Allah, if you were a god, you and a dog would not be together in a well tied in disgrace!" Thus, he entered the religion of Allah.

Amr tasted the sweetness of faith and embraced the new religion with his heart, body, wealth, and children. When the Battle of Uhud arrived, he saw his three sons preparing for battle, and his yearning for martyrdom surged. He was an elderly man with a severe limp, and Allah the Almighty had excused him from Jihad. His sons tried to stop him, but he grew angry and rushed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to complain about them, saying: "O Prophet of Allah, these sons of mine wish to keep me from this goodness, using the excuse that I am lame. By Allah, I truly hope to tread into Paradise with this lame foot of mine!" The Prophet ﷺ said to his sons: "Leave him; perhaps Allah the Almighty will grant him martyrdom."

Amr bid his wife farewell like one who departs and does not return, raising his palms to the sky and supplicating: "O Allah, grant me martyrdom and do not return me to my family disappointed." Then he set out, surrounded by his sons and his people. When the fierce heat of battle ignited, Amr ibn al-Jamuh was seen leaping on his sound leg, saying: "I am longing for Paradise, I am longing for Paradise!" He continued fighting valiantly in defense of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until he fell stricken as a martyr alongside his son Khallad. The Prophet ﷺ commanded that Amr ibn al-Jamuh be buried with Abdullah ibn Amr, for they had loved and cherished one another in this world.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The power of sincere faith which eradicates all attachment to falsehood and drives a person to sacrifice everything precious and valuable.
2. The importance of the role of children in calling their parents to the truth with wisdom and beautiful preaching.
3. The immense yearning for martyrdom in the path of Allah, and how sincere intention transcends physical barriers.
4. The mercy and wisdom of the Prophet ﷺ in dealing with the sincere desires of the Companions, even when they went beyond legal excuses.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: What are the "idols" of our lives that we cling to, which prevent us from fully dedicating ourselves to the obedience of Allah, and how can we rid ourselves of them?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Identify a negative habit or a worldly attachment that weighs you down from obedience, and strive earnestly to rid yourself of it today, seeking the help of Allah the Almighty.

title: The Eternal Supplication for Martyrdom
subtitle: The journey of a noble Companion who traded his worldly life for Allah and purchased His Paradise, becoming the first person to have a banner tied for him in Islam.
heroQuote: "O Allah, grant me a fierce opponent with intense wrath and might; I will fight him for Your sake and he will fight me, then he will overpower me and sever my nose and my ear. Then, when I meet You tomorrow, You will ask: 'For what were your nose and ear severed?' And I will say: 'For You and Your Messenger.' And You will say: 'You have spoken the truth.'"
intention: Read today's journey to ponder the greatness of sacrifice in the path of Allah and His Messenger, and what sincerity in seeking martyrdom looks like.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi was a noble Companion closely related to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ—he was the son of his paternal aunt, Umaymah bint Abd al-Muttalib, and his brother-in-law, as his sister Zaynab bint Jahsh was the wife of the noble Prophet and one of the Mothers of the Believers. He was among the foremost precursors to Islam, having embraced it before the Prophet ﷺ entered the house of Al-Arqam, and was among the early emigrants to Abyssinia and then to Medina, prioritizing his religion over every precious and valuable thing.

steps.type: Fulfilling the Home and Seeking Martyrdom
steps.title: Fulfilling the Home and Seeking Martyrdom
steps.content:
When the Prophet ﷺ permitted his Companions to migrate to Medina, fleeing with their religion from the persecution of Quraysh, Abdullah ibn Jahsh (May Allah be pleased with him) was the second immigrant after Abu Salamah. This migration was unlike his previous one to Abyssinia; it was broader and more comprehensive, as he migrated with his family, relatives, and paternal kin—men and women alike—leaving behind his home, which was one of the most beautiful and affluent houses in Makkah.

No sooner had he departed from Makkah than Abu Jahl seized his house and disposed of it as its rightful owner. When Abdullah learned of this, his soul found peace and his eyes were comforted when the Prophet ﷺ gave him the glad tidings, saying: "Are you not pleased, O Abdullah, that Allah will give you in exchange a house in Paradise?" He replied, "Indeed, O Messenger of Allah," and the Prophet said, "Then it is yours."

Hardly had Abdullah settled in Medina when the Prophet ﷺ appointed him to lead the first military expedition in Islam, known as the Expedition of Nakhlah. The Prophet ﷺ tied the banner for him, making him the first commander over a group of believers. The Prophet ﷺ instructed him not to look into the written letter until he had traveled for two days. When he looked at it, he found the order to march to 'Nakhlah' to intercept a Qurayshi caravan. The Companions consulted one another regarding fighting the caravan during the sacred months, realizing that fighting therein was a major offense, and they killed one man and captured two.

Initially, the Prophet ﷺ disapproved of their action, but Allah revealed a Quranic verse clarifying the matter: ﴿They ask you about fighting in the sacred month. Say, 'Fighting therein is great [sin], but hindering [people] from the way of Allah and disbelief in Him and [preventing access to] al-Masjid al-Haram and the expulsion of its people therefrom are greater in the sight of Allah . And fitnah is greater than killing.'﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 217). Thus, the Companions rejoiced, and the heart of the Prophet ﷺ found peace.

In the Battle of Uhud, Abdullah ibn Jahsh met his companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (May Allah be pleased with them), and they offered a magnificent supplication. Sa'd prayed that Allah grant him a man of fierce might to fight him, whom he would kill and take his spoils, and Abdullah amen-ed his supplication. Then Abdullah supplicated, saying: "O Allah, grant me a fierce opponent with intense wrath and might; I will fight him for Your sake and he will fight me, then he will overpower me and sever my nose and my ear. Then, when I meet You tomorrow, You will ask: 'For what were your nose and ear severed?' And I will say: 'For You and Your Messenger.' And You will say: 'You have spoken the truth.'" Allah answered his prayer; he fought until he was martyred and his body was mutilated, with his nose and ear found tied with a string. The Prophet ﷺ buried him alongside his maternal uncle Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib in a single grave, his pure tears watering the soil drenched in the fragrances of martyrdom.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The greatness of sacrificing wealth and homeland in the path of Allah, and that the recompense is of the same nature as the deed—whoever leaves something for the sake of Allah, Allah replaces it with something better in this world and the Hereafter.
2. The importance of obeying those in authority, even if a command seems difficult or unclear at the time, for the ultimate outcome belongs to the righteous.
3. Sincerity of intention in seeking martyrdom, and how Allah answers the supplication of the truthful in His path.
4. Steadfastness upon principles and firm faith, even in the most severe and difficult circumstances, and that persecution in religion is worse than killing.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: What are you willing to sacrifice for the sake of your religion? And do your supplications to Allah reflect the sincerity of your intention and your desire to attain His pleasure and Paradise?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Give charity today purely for the sake of Allah, or perform a volunteer act, bringing to mind the intention of sacrifice in the path of Allah, and sincerely ask Allah for martyrdom.

title: The Trustworthy of the Ummah and Its Ransom
subtitle: The journey of the Trustworthy of this Ummah, who offered his soul and his teeth as a ransom for his faith and his Prophet ﷺ, exemplifying the highest standards of trust and faith.
heroQuote: "Every nation has a trustworthy one, and you are the trustworthy one of this nation." - Statement of the Prophet ﷺ.
intention: Read today's journey to draw inspiration from the Trustworthy of the Ummah regarding the loftiest meanings of trustworthiness and sacrifice for the sake of truth, and how sincere faith is manifested.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Abu Ubaydah عامر bin 'Abdullah bin al-Jarrah al-Fihri al-Qurashi was the trustworthy one of this Ummah by the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He was bright-faced, radiant in appearance, slender in body, tall, with light cheeks. The eye rested upon the sight of him, and the soul found comfort in his presence. He was soft-spoken, immensely humble, and deeply modest; yet when matters grew grave and earnestness was required, he moved like a charging lion. He embraced Islam on the day following the Islam of Abu Bakr as-Siddiq (May Allah be pleased with him), and was among the foremost precursors to Islam who remained steadfast in their religion despite severe persecution and trials in Makkah.

steps.title: Between Trust and Sacrifice
steps.content:
Abu Ubaydah (May Allah be pleased with him) lived through the harsh trials of the Muslims in Makkah, remaining steadfast and proving true to Allah and His Messenger in every situation. However, his trial on the Day of Badr surpassed all imagination, as he was forced to kill his own father, who was fighting in the ranks of the polytheists. Abu Ubaydah did not kill his father; rather, he killed polytheism personified in his father. Consequently, Allah the Almighty revealed regarding him and his father: {You will not find a people who believe in Allah and the Last Day having affection for those who oppose Allah and His Messenger, even if they were their fathers or their sons or their brothers or their kindred...} (Al-Mujadila: 22).

His strength and trustworthiness manifested on numerous occasions, including the day the Messenger ﷺ sent him as a commander over a group of his companions to intercept a caravan of Quraysh, providing them with a small leather pouch containing dates, as he found nothing else for them. Abu Ubaydah would give each of his companions a single date a day, which he would suck upon just as a baby sucks upon its mother's breast, drinking water afterwards, which sufficed him from morning until night.

On the Day of Uhud, when the Muslims were defeated and a herald of the polytheists began shouting, "Show me Muhammad," Abu Ubaydah was one of the ten who surrounded the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to shield him with their chests. When the battle concluded, and the Prophet ﷺ had his lower incisor broken, his forehead gashed, and two rings of his helmet embedded into his cheek, Abu Bakr came forward to extract them. However, Abu Ubaydah pleaded with him to leave the task to him. Fearing he might cause pain to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ if he pulled them out with his hands, Abu Ubaydah bit down firmly on the first ring with his incisor and pulled it out, causing his own incisor to fall. Then he bit down on the second ring with his second incisor and extracted it, causing his second incisor to fall. Thus, he became one of the finest toothless men.

Following the death of the Prophet ﷺ, on the Day of Saqifah, Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him) offered to pledge allegiance to him as Caliph, saying: "Stretch out your hand so I may pledge allegiance to you, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Every nation has a trustworthy one, and you are the trustworthy one of this nation.'" But out of profound humility and scrupulousness, Abu Ubaydah refused, saying: "I would not put myself forward before a man whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered to lead us in prayer, and he led us until he passed away." Thus, he remained the finest counselor to Abu Bakr as-Siddiq and his most noble assistant in righteousness.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. Absolute trustworthiness in religion and worldly affairs, and how it is a comprehensive virtue that made Abu Ubaydah the trustworthy one of the Ummah.
2. Prioritizing the love of Allah and His Messenger over every relationship, even that of fatherhood, as seen in his attitude toward his father on the Day of Badr.
3. Physical and psychological sacrifice to protect the Prophet ﷺ and defend the faith, as he did at Uhud.
4. Immense humility and asceticism regarding leadership positions, preferring the one who is more deserving and superior, as demonstrated on the Day of Saqifah.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.content: Are you trustworthy regarding what has been entrusted to you in your life? And how can you prioritize the love of Allah and His Messenger over everything else in your daily decisions?

steps.title: Today's Action
steps.content: Review your trusts and responsibilities, and strive to fulfill them in the most complete manner, mindful that you are entrusted with them before Allah. Reflect upon a moment when you prioritized the love of Allah and His Messenger over your own desires.

title: Keeper of the Secret and Treasure of the Quran
subtitle: The journey of a young shepherd who transformed into a servant of the Prophet ﷺ and became one of the most proficient companions in reciting and knowing the Book of Allah.
heroQuote: "Whoever is pleased to recite the Quran fresh as it was revealed, let him recite it according to the recitation of Ibn Umm Abd."
intention: Read today's journey to ponder the greatness of knowledge of the Quran, sincerity in serving the religion, and courage in proclaiming the truth.

steps.title: Introduction
steps.content: Abdullah ibn Masud al-Hudhali (May Allah be pleased with him) was, in his early youth, a young shepherd grazing sheep for one of the dignitaries of Quraysh, Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt, in the valleys of Makkah away from the bustle of people. He was known as 'Ibn Umm Abd', and little did he know that destiny held a magnificent status for him, and that a single encounter would alter the course of his life forever, making him one of the leading scholars and reciters of the Muslims.

steps.type: From Shepherd to Servant of the Prophet and Scholar of the Quran
steps.title: From Shepherd to Servant of the Prophet and Scholar of the Quran
steps.content:
One day, while Abdullah was grazing his sheep, he saw two dignified elderly men approaching him, exhausted from thirst. They greeted him and asked him to milk one of his sheep for them to drink. The youth replied honestly: "I will not do so; the sheep are not mine, and I am entrusted with them." The two men did not object to his words; rather, satisfaction appeared upon them. Then one of them said: "Show me a young ewe that has not been approached by a ram." Abdullah pointed to a small ewe. The man stepped forward, held it, and began passing his hand over its udder while mentioning the name of Allah. The youth was astonished as the ewe's udder swelled and milk flowed abundantly. The other man filled a hollow stone with milk, and he and his companion drank, then gave the youth a drink. When he had quenched his thirst, the blessed man said to the ewe's udder, "Contract," and it contracted until it returned to its original state. Thereupon, the youth asked the man to teach him some of these words, and he replied, "You are a taught youth."

The blessed man was none other than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and his companion was the truthful Abu Bakr (May Allah be pleased with him). That was the beginning of Abdullah ibn Masud's story with Islam. Abdullah accompanied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ like a shadow, joining him in his travels and residing with him, serving him in his home and abroad, until he was called the "Keeper of the Secret of the Messenger of Allah." He followed his guidance and adopted his character to the extent that it was said of him: "He is the closest of people in guidance and demeanor to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

Ibn Masud was among the companions who recited the Quran most proficiently and understood its meanings best. Umar ibn al-Khattab (May Allah be pleased with him) bore witness to his knowledge. One night, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr, and Umar were conversing, they heard a man praying in the mosque (Ibn Masud). The Prophet ﷺ listened to him and then said: "Whoever is pleased to recite the Quran fresh as it was revealed, let him recite it according to the recitation of Ibn Umm Abd." Then he called Abdullah, and the Prophet ﷺ began saying to him: "Ask and you shall be given, ask and you shall be given." Umar rushed to convey the good news to him, only to find that Abu Bakr had already preceded him. Abdullah used to say: "By the One besides Whom there is no god, no verse was revealed in the Book of Allah except that I know where it was revealed and concerning what it was revealed."

His knowledge was not limited to recitation; rather, he was courageous and valiant. It is enough that he was the first Muslim to openly recite the Quran in Makkah after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. One day, the vulnerable companions of the Prophet gathered and said: "By Allah, Quraysh has never heard this Quran being recited aloud openly. Who is the man who will let them hear it?" Abdullah said, "I will let them hear it." He went to the mosque near the Station of Ibrahim and recited Surah Ar-Rahman, raising his voice. Quraysh rose up against him, striking his face while he continued to recite until he reached what Allah willed he should reach. Then he returned to his companions with blood flowing from him. They said to him, "This is what we feared for you." He replied, "By Allah, the enemies of Allah are not more insignificant in my eyes than they are right now, and if you wish, I will confront them with the like of it tomorrow."

Abdullah ibn Masud lived until the era of the Caliphate of Uthman (May Allah be pleased with him). When he fell terminally ill, Uthman came to visit him and asked, "What do you complain of?" He replied, "My sins." Uthman asked, "And what do you desire?" He replied, "The mercy of my Lord." Uthman offered him a stipend that he had refused to accept for years. Abdullah said, "I have no need for it." Uthman said, "It will be for your daughters after you." Abdullah said, "Do you fear poverty for my daughters? I have commanded them to recite Surah Al-Waqi'ah every night, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'Whoever recites Al-Waqi'ah every night will never be afflicted by poverty.'" When night fell, Abdullah ibn Masud joined the Highest Company, his tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah and fresh with His clear verses.

steps.title: Lessons Learned
steps.content:
1. The virtue of knowledge of the Quran, reflecting upon it, and the importance of specializing in it.
2. Sincerity in serving the Prophet ﷺ and the religion, and diligence in seeking knowledge.
3. Courage in proclaiming the truth and calling to it, even if it leads to harm.
4. Asceticism in worldly life, reliance upon Allah, and trust in His promise of provision.

steps.title: Reflection
